note: Fits the profile on everything except the one criterion that decided the call. MATCHES: 'successful' — software engineer who builds products and also does financial work and trading, and who sends his children to a fee-paying school; not literally a business owner or physician but a reasonable read of 'or equivalent'. 'Neglected_health' — no crisis anywhere, just a decades-long on-off pattern; textbook. 'Good_to_great' — he is not being rescued, he swings a 32 kg bell, plays basketball with his kids and hikes long distance; he wants to remove a belly and stop cycling. 'Not_deconditioned' — emphatically the opposite of the excluded 50-lb-overweight gym-averse profile. MISS: 'income' — and it is decisive. He said the household situation is 'a little shaky in some ways', that private school fees take up most of the budget, and that he has never spent this much on a coach in his life. He was not able to say yes at $6,000. This is the same shape as the Badrane Hriouch assessment already on file — fits on profile, fails on willingness or ability to pay — with one instructive difference in how it was handled. On that call the rep recognised the mismatch live and disqualified rather than discounted. On this call the rep discounted, inventing a $3,000 tier rather than either qualifying the prospect out or building the value case. Two prospects, the same ICP failure mode, opposite rep behaviour and a $3,000 spread in the outcome. That divergence is the finding worth escalating from this record, and it argues that 'makes good money' is not currently functioning as a screen at all — it is functioning as a discount trigger.
